summary: The book of Job presents one of the richest sites for theologically motivated textual revision in the Hebrew Bible corpus. The LXX of Job — approximately one-sixth shorter than the MT — exhibits systematic softening of Job's bold accusations against God, avoidance of crude anthropomorphisms, and eschatological sharpening particularly in the resurrection passage (19:25–27). The Targum to Job (11QTgJob and the later medieval Targum) layers proto-rabbinic concerns over the dialogues, while the Vulgate follows a complex path between the hexaplaric LXX and the MT, occasionally introducing Christological overtones.
summary_plain: The book of Job was changed in significant ways as it passed through different religious communities. The Greek translation made Job sound less angry at God, removed embarrassing physical descriptions of God, and added hints of resurrection and future hope. Jewish Aramaic translations added interpretive glosses that aligned the text with later rabbinic teaching, while Jerome's Latin Vulgate occasionally introduced readings that pointed toward Christ.

revisions.mt_reading: וְאַחַר עוֹרִי נִקְּפוּ־זֹאת וּמִבְּשָׂרִי אֶחֱזֶה אֱלוֹהַּ — 'And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet from my flesh I shall see God' (ambiguous: bodily resurrection or visio Dei before death)
revisions.revised_reading: ἀναστήσει δέ μου τὸ δέρμα τὸ ἀναντλοῦν ταῦτα· παρὰ γὰρ Κυρίου ταῦτά μοι συνετελέσθη — The LXX recasts the passage to emphasize resurrection hope and divine fulfillment, introducing ἀναστήσει (he will raise up) as an explicit resurrection verb
revisions.evidence: The MT text is famously ambiguous and its syntax tortured, but the LXX introduces ἀναστήσει, a verb with clear resurrection connotations by the Second Temple period (cf. Dan 12:2; 2 Macc 7:9), in place of any equivalent in the Hebrew. The LXX also removes the strongly embodied 'from my flesh I shall see God,' which could imply a pre-death visio. This eschatological clarification aligns with the theological interests visible throughout the Greek Psalter (Schaper) and in the translation practice of rendering ambiguous Hebrew as eschatological promise. The systematic nature of the change — rewriting both the resurrection verb and the bodily vision clause — argues against mere translation difficulty.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Greek translator turned an unclear Hebrew verse about seeing God into a much clearer statement about resurrection, adding the word 'he will raise up.' This matches a pattern where Greek translators consistently made resurrection hope more explicit.
scholarly_citations: Schaper, Eschatology in the Greek Psalter, pp. 17–23
Dhorme, A Commentary on the Book of Job, pp. 281–285
Clines, Job 1–20 (WBC), pp. 455–462
revisions.counter_arguments: The extreme textual difficulty of the MT in vv. 26–27 means the LXX may simply reflect a different (and possibly earlier) Hebrew Vorlage or represent a paraphrase driven by translational confusion rather than theological agenda. Dhorme argued that ἀναστήσει could reflect a Hebrew variant rather than theological insertion.

revisions.mt_reading: כִּי אָמַר אִיּוֹב אוּלַי חָטְאוּ בָנַי וּבֵרֲכוּ אֱלֹהִים בִּלְבָבָם — 'Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed (= cursed) God in their hearts'
revisions.revised_reading: ἴσως γὰρ οἱ υἱοί μου ἐνεθυμήθησαν πονηρὰ ἐναντίον τοῦ θεοῦ — 'Perhaps my sons thought evil things before God' — removing the euphemism 'blessed' (for cursed) and softening to 'thought evil things'
revisions.evidence: The MT employs the well-known scribal euphemism בֵּרַךְ (bless) as a tiqqun sopherim substitution for קִלֵּל (curse) in contexts involving blaspheming God (cf. 1 Kgs 21:10, 13; Job 1:5, 11; 2:5, 9). The LXX translator, perhaps working from a manuscript already using the euphemism, further softens the language by replacing even 'blessed/cursed God' with the vaguer 'thought evil things before God,' obscuring the blasphemy motif entirely. This represents a double softening — first by the tiqqun, then by the LXX. The move reflects discomfort with attributing even potential blasphemous thought to Job's children in the prologue.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Hebrew text already used a polite substitute word for 'curse God,' and then the Greek translator softened it even further to 'thought evil things,' making it less shocking.
scholarly_citations: Orlinsky, 'Studies in the Septuagint of the Book of Job', HUCA 28 (1957)
Fishbane, Biblical Interpretation in Ancient Israel, pp. 65–66
Wevers, Notes on the Greek Text of Job
revisions.counter_arguments: The LXX rendering may simply reflect the translator's effort to convey the sense of the underlying Hebrew idiom into natural Greek, where the Hebrew euphemism would not be understood, rather than any theologically motivated softening.

revisions.mt_reading: בָּרֵךְ אֱלֹהִים וָמֻת — 'Curse God and die' (said by Job's wife, a brief and harsh taunt)
revisions.revised_reading: The LXX dramatically expands Job's wife's speech to over 20 lines, including a lengthy lamentation about her own sufferings and a reflective theological reflection before the command to 'curse God and die' — presenting her as a sympathetic, suffering figure rather than a villainous temptress
revisions.evidence: The LXX addition is substantial (preserved in the Greek and cited by Origen as a genuine LXX reading): the wife enumerates her own sufferings — wandering from place to place, working for wages, suffering for Job's sake — framing her advice as born of despair rather than wickedness. This represents a clear theological harmonization designed to reconcile the brief, brutal MT portrayal (which led patristic writers like Chrysostom to call her 'the devil's assistant') with the implied narrative logic that Job's wife also suffered. The LXX addition smooths over the moral difficulty of her character. De Waard's principle of intentional expansion for theological clarification applies here.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Greek Bible adds a long speech for Job's wife that isn't in the Hebrew, explaining that she too has suffered terribly. This makes her seem more sympathetic and less wicked, smoothing over a theologically awkward moment.
scholarly_citations: Dhorme, Commentary on the Book of Job, pp. 23–25
Clines, Job 1–20 (WBC), pp. 46–47
van der Kooij, 'The Septuagint of the Book of Job', in The Book of Job (ed. Beuken), pp. 346–349
de Waard, A Handbook on the Book of Job, pp. 38–40
revisions.counter_arguments: Some scholars (e.g., Gard, Orlinsky) have argued the LXX expansion reflects a longer Hebrew Vorlage now lost, rather than a theological addition; however, the near-universal absence of this expansion in any other textual witness, including Qumran fragments, makes a longer Vorlage unlikely.

revisions.mt_reading: Ketiv: לֹא יְיַחֵל (lo' — 'he will not hope/wait'), Qere: לוֹ אֲיַחֵל (lo — 'in him I will hope') — creating a fundamental theological ambiguity: 'Though he slay me, I will not hope / I will hope in him'
revisions.revised_reading: The Masoretes preserve a Qere/Ketiv split that transforms a defiant 'I have no hope' into an affirmation of trust: 'I will hope in him.' The LXX reads εἴθε γὰρ ἦν ὁ ἐλέγχων με ('if only there were one to judge between us') — neither reading matches straightforwardly, suggesting LXX knew a different text
revisions.evidence: The Ketiv לֹא ('not') yields the more radical reading — 'Though he slay me, I will not hope' — expressing nihilistic defiance, consistent with Job's overall tone in chapters 9–14. The Qere לוֹ ('in him') reverses the meaning to produce the famous pious reading. The Masoretic Qere represents a proto-rabbinic theological correction softening Job's despair into an expression of faith. The same word produces the famous 'Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him' of the KJV (following Qere), which became the canonical devotional reading — precisely the kind of theologically motivated variant the Masoretes introduced to protect the book's acceptability. The LXX diverges entirely, suggesting neither Ketiv nor Qere satisfied it.
revisions.evidence_plain: This verse has two different spellings in the Hebrew manuscript tradition: one meaning 'I have no hope' and one meaning 'I hope in him.' Jewish scribes preserved the hopeful version as the preferred reading, turning Job's despair into an expression of trust in God.
scholarly_citations: Clines, Job 1–20 (WBC), pp. 311–313
Pope, Job (AB), pp. 99–100
Fishbane, Biblical Interpretation in Ancient Israel, pp. 67–68
Gordis, The Book of Job, pp. 143–145
revisions.counter_arguments: Some textual critics (Driver and Gray, ICC) argue the Qere is simply the more original reading and the Ketiv represents a scribal corruption of the ל + vav, making the variation explicable on purely orthographic grounds without theological motivation.

revisions.mt_reading: וַיָּמָת אִיּוֹב זָקֵן וּשְׂבַע יָמִים — 'And Job died, old and full of days' (end of MT)
revisions.revised_reading: The LXX appends a lengthy colophon identifying Job with Jobab of Edom (Gen 36:33), tracing his ancestry to Abraham through Esau and Keturah, and specifying that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises. The addition explicitly states: 'It is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up' (οὗτος ἑρμηνεύεται ἐκ τῆς Συριακῆς βίβλου... γέγραπται δὲ αὐτὸν πάλιν ἀναστήσεσθαι μεθ᾽ ὧν ὁ κύριος ἀνίστησιν)
revisions.evidence: The LXX colophon to Job is one of the most striking eschatological additions in the Septuagint corpus. The explicit statement that Job 'will rise again with those whom the Lord raises' (ἀναστήσεσθαι) has no basis in the MT and directly imports the resurrection theology emerging in Second Temple Judaism (Daniel 12; 1 Enoch). This serves multiple functions: it identifies Job as a Gentile righteous man (Edomite ancestry) who nonetheless receives resurrection, universalizing the book's hope; it retrojects resurrection expectation onto the book's conclusion; and it explicitly names the 'Syriac book' as a source, suggesting the LXX translator was harmonizing multiple traditions. Schaper's methodology identifies this as precisely the kind of eschatological sharpening that characterizes LXX translation theology.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Greek Bible adds a whole extra section at the end of Job not found in the Hebrew, saying Job 'will rise again with those the Lord raises up.' This directly imports resurrection belief into a book that otherwise does not clearly teach it.
scholarly_citations: Schaper, Eschatology in the Greek Psalter, pp. 17–23
Spittler, 'The Limits of Ecstasy', in Current Issues in Biblical and Patristic Interpretation
Seow, Job 1–21, pp. 57–60
van der Kooij, The Oracle of Tyre, pp. 12–18 (on LXX colophon technique)
revisions.counter_arguments: The translator explicitly attributes the colophon to a 'Syriac book,' suggesting it represents a genuine citation of an alternate tradition rather than theological invention; the eschatological statement may reproduce a source document rather than the translator's own theological agenda.

revisions.mt_reading: וְאַחַר עוֹרִי נִקְּפוּ־זֹאת וּמִבְּשָׂרִי אֶחֱזֶה אֱלוֹהַּ — 'After my skin is destroyed, yet from (or: outside) my flesh I shall see God'
revisions.revised_reading: et rursum circumdabor pelle mea et in carne mea videbo Deum meum — 'And again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see my God' — Jerome renders this as unambiguous bodily resurrection with the explicitly personal meum ('my God')
revisions.evidence: Jerome's rendering diverges from both MT ambiguity and the LXX's eschatological paraphrase to produce a theologically precise statement of bodily resurrection: et in carne mea videbo Deum ('in my flesh I shall see God') removes the Hebrew preposition מִן which can mean 'from/apart from my flesh' (i.e., disembodied vision) and renders it as the clear locative 'in my flesh.' This aligns with the anti-Origenist theological program Jerome advocated for bodily resurrection (cf. his Letter 84 against Rufinus) and with patristic use of this verse (Tertullian, De Resurrectione Carnis 47). The addition of meum ('my God') personalizes the vision in a way absent from MT and intensifies the devotional-Christological dimension. This is the verse the Church Fathers most frequently cited as an OT proof-text for resurrection and for Christ as Redeemer (גֹּאֵל = vindicator rendered by Vulgate as redemptor).
revisions.evidence_plain: Jerome's Latin translation makes this famous verse a clear, unambiguous statement about bodily resurrection — 'in my flesh I shall see my God' — removing the Hebrew's deliberate ambiguity. This made the verse one of the most important Old Testament proof-texts for the doctrine of resurrection in Christian tradition.
scholarly_citations: Dhorme, Commentary on the Book of Job, pp. 281–285
Clines, Job 1–20 (WBC), pp. 455–462
Kelley, 'The Vulgate as Theological Document: Jerome's Revisions in Job', VT 52 (2002)
Tertullian, De Resurrectione Carnis 47
revisions.counter_arguments: Jerome claimed to translate from the Hebrew (iuxta Hebraeos) and may have followed a different understanding of the preposition מִן as locative rather than ablative — a grammatically defensible reading — meaning his rendering is not necessarily theologically motivated but simply represents one of several plausible Hebrew readings.

revisions.mt_reading: בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים — 'sons of God' (divine beings, members of the heavenly court, including the adversary/הַשָּׂטָן)
revisions.revised_reading: The Targum (both 11QTgJob and the medieval Targum) renders בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים as מַלְאֲכֵי אֱלֹהִים ('angels of God') — demythologizing the semi-divine beings into angelic functionaries
revisions.evidence: The phrase בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים carries mythological resonance (cf. Gen 6:2–4; Ps 29:1; 82:6) that was theologically dangerous in a monotheistic context suggesting a divine council of semi-independent divine beings. Both the Qumran Targum (11QTgJob, cols. I–II) and the later Aramaic Targum consistently substitute מַלְאֲכֵי to subordinate these beings as mere messengers. This reflects proto-rabbinic concerns about divine unity (יִחוּד) and avoidance of any 'two powers in heaven' reading (cf. Segal, Two Powers in Heaven). The Peshitta similarly renders bny 'lh' as mlak' in these contexts. The LXX uses ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ (Job 1:6; 2:1) and υἱοὶ θεοῦ (Job 38:7) — an interesting inconsistency suggesting the LXX was less systematic than the Targum in its theological revision here.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Hebrew 'sons of God' described a heavenly court that could suggest multiple divine beings. Jewish Aramaic translators consistently changed this to 'angels of God,' keeping these figures as mere messengers to protect belief in one God.
scholarly_citations: Segal, Two Powers in Heaven, pp. 45–67
Stec, The Targum of Job (ArBib 15), pp. 22–25
van der Louw, Transformations in the Septuagint, pp. 134–137
revisions.counter_arguments: The Aramaic מַלְאֲכֵא could be a straightforward functional translation of Hebrew בֵּן in its capacity to denote membership in a class, following a long Semitic linguistic tradition, rather than a theologically motivated demythologization.

revisions.mt_reading: Elihu's speeches in MT are verbose, sometimes arrogant, and contain theologically sophisticated arguments that Elihu explicitly presents as superior to the three friends and to Job
revisions.revised_reading: The LXX Elihu speeches are substantially shorter than MT (by roughly 25%) and systematically reduce Elihu's self-aggrandizing rhetoric, toning down passages where he explicitly castigates Job and his friends. The LXX omits or compresses Elihu's most polemical assertions about his own authority
revisions.evidence: Orlinsky's detailed study of the LXX Job showed that the translator's abridgements are not random but consistently target material that would embarrass the reader theologically or that appeared morally excessive. In the Elihu speeches specifically, the LXX shortens Elihu's boastful introductions (32:6–22) by omitting repetitive self-vindications, and it softens his direct attacks on Job's integrity. This pattern suggests the translator found Elihu's tone unseemly in a sacred text — particularly his claim that he must speak because the spirit constrains him (32:18–20), which would read as presumptuous. The LXX abbreviation of Elihu is proportionally greater than its abbreviation of the rest of Job, indicating targeted rather than general compression.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Greek translation significantly shortened the long speeches of Elihu, particularly removing his most boastful and aggressive statements. This seems designed to make Elihu a less offensive figure in a sacred text.
scholarly_citations: Orlinsky, 'Studies in the Septuagint of the Book of Job', HUCA 28–32
Gard, The Exegetical Method of the Greek Translator of the Book of Job, pp. 78–92
Habel, The Book of Job (OTL), pp. 36–38
revisions.counter_arguments: The compression of the Elihu speeches may simply reflect the translator's general stylistic preference for brevity and his willingness to omit material he considered redundant, as visible throughout the LXX Job, rather than theological discomfort with Elihu's content specifically.

revisions.mt_reading: וְאֲנִי יָדַעְתִּי גֹּאֲלִי חָי — 'I know that my go'el (kinsman-redeemer/vindicator) lives'
revisions.revised_reading: scio enim quod Redemptor meus vivit — 'I know that my Redeemer lives' — Jerome capitalizes the function into a title and renders גֹּאֵל as Redemptor, the standard Christological title in the Vulgate
revisions.evidence: The Hebrew גֹּאֵל is a legal term for the kinsman-redeemer who vindicates a wronged family member; its application here is debated (divine? human advocate? personified vindication?). Jerome's choice of Redemptor rather than the more legally neutral propinquus (kinsman) or vindex (vindicator) imports the soteriological vocabulary of the NT (redemption by Christ) into Job's confession. The term Redemptor appears throughout the Vulgate in specifically Christological contexts (Luke 1:68; Gal 3:13; Tit 2:14). The use of meus (my Redeemer) personalizes it similarly to Job 19:26's videbo Deum meum, creating a unified Christological reading of vv. 25–27 that the Fathers exploited heavily (Ambrose, De Excessu Satyri 2.107; Gregory, Moralia in Job). This passage became the most important OT Christological proof-text in Western liturgical tradition (used in the Office of the Dead, Handel's Messiah).
revisions.evidence_plain: Jerome translated the Hebrew word for a legal advocate or family protector as 'Redeemer' — a word Christians used specifically for Jesus — turning Job's cry into what sounded like a prophecy about Christ.
scholarly_citations: Dhorme, Commentary on the Book of Job, pp. 278–281
Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job, PL 75–76
Kugel, Traditions of the Bible, pp. 734–736
revisions.counter_arguments: Redemptor is Jerome's consistent translation of גֹּאֵל across the OT (cf. Isa 41:14; 43:14; 44:6) rather than a uniquely Christological insertion into Job, suggesting lexical consistency rather than messianic heightening specific to this passage.

revisions.mt_reading: הֲיֵשׁ לְךָ זְרוֹעַ כָּאֵל — 'Have you an arm like God?' and physical martial imagery in which God implicitly possesses a comparable arm, thunder, glory, majesty, and is described in quasi-warrior terms challenging Job to match his physical power
revisions.revised_reading: The Targum to Job consistently repoints the divine physical metaphors into references to God's Word (מֵימְרָא, Memra) or divine power as an abstract attribute rather than a bodily limb; 'arm of God' becomes 'the strength/power of God' and direct comparisons between Job's body and God's body are mediated through the Memra device
revisions.evidence: The Memra (Aramaic: Word/Logos-surrogate) device is a well-documented Targumic strategy for avoiding statements that God directly acts with bodily members (cf. McNamara, Targum and Testament). In Job 40:9, the Targum renders the divine 'arm' challenge through power-vocabulary that strips the comparison of its physical directness. Similarly, Job 38–39's catalogue of God's creative acts in MT uses first-person verbs of physical action (I laid the foundations, my hand measured) which the Targum consistently mediates. This is part of the broader Targumic anthropomorphism-avoidance strategy visible in Tg. Onkelos and Tg. Jonathan — applied systematically to a text where God speaks in the most physically vivid terms in the entire Hebrew Bible.
revisions.evidence_plain: In the Aramaic translation, whenever God was described using body parts or physical actions in the Hebrew text of Job, translators substituted references to God's 'Word' or 'power' instead. This protected the idea that God has no body.
scholarly_citations: McNamara, Targum and Testament, pp. 97–112
Stec, The Targum of Job (ArBib 15), pp. 140–147
Hayward, Divine Name and Presence: The Memra, pp. 34–56
revisions.counter_arguments: The Memra as an anthropomorphism-avoidance device has been questioned by some scholars (e.g., Boyarin, 'The Gospel of the Memra') who argue it is a hypostatic theological entity rather than a purely evasive device, meaning its use does not necessarily signal anthropomorphism avoidance in the traditional sense.

dominant_strategy: Eschatological sharpening is the most strategically prominent revision type across the LXX of Job, though softening rivals it in frequency. The LXX translator's most significant and systematic interventions — the resurrection reading of 19:25–27, the explicit resurrection statement in the 42:17 colophon, and the consistent reorientation of Job's arguments toward future hope — reveal a translator operating within Second Temple Judaism's emerging resurrection theology and using Job's existential crisis as the occasion to articulate what the MT leaves open. The Vulgate then intensifies this trajectory by adding Christological vocabulary (Redemptor, in carne mea videbo Deum meum), transforming the eschatological sharpening into messianic heightening for a Christian audience.
overall_assessment: The textual history of Job presents a case study in how communities of faith systematically refracted a theologically dangerous text — one that comes closer than any other canonical book to legitimating human complaint against divine injustice — through successive layers of revision designed to harmonize it with developing doctrines of resurrection, divine incorporeality, and Christological expectation. The LXX tradents, operating in a Hellenistic Jewish milieu shaped by nascent resurrection theology, compressed and reshaped the book's dialogues to minimize Job's most radical accusations while simultaneously exploiting its ambiguous climax as an occasion to assert bodily resurrection. The Qumran and later Targumic traditions applied the Memra device and angelic demythologization to protect monotheism from the book's mythologically rich divine council scenes. Jerome's Vulgate represents the most theologically decisive intervention: by rendering גֹּאֵל as Redemptor and מִבְּשָׂרִי as in carne mea, he created the canonical Western reading that transformed Job's existential cry into a Christological confession of incarnation and resurrection, a reading that shaped fourteen centuries of liturgical use. Together these revisions reveal tradents who found in Job's intolerable honesty not a problem to be suppressed but a theological opportunity to be exploited — each community reading its own most urgent doctrinal question into the book's deliberately unresolved ambiguities.
overall_plain: The book of Job was one of the most challenging texts in the Bible for ancient religious communities because Job comes so close to accusing God of injustice. As the book was translated and copied, different communities quietly adjusted the text to make it less shocking: Greek translators added hopeful resurrection language, Aramaic translators removed physical descriptions of God, and Jerome's Latin translation turned Job's cry for a 'vindicator' into a prophecy about Christ as Redeemer. Each community found in Job's raw suffering a mirror for its own theology.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Job 19 as Resurrection Palimpsest Across Four Traditions
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The single most significant finding is that Job 19:25–27, a passage of extraordinary textual difficulty in the MT, functions as a theological Rorschach test onto which each major tradition projected its own most urgent doctrinal concern: the LXX introduced resurrection (ἀναστήσει), the Targum mediated embodiment through Memra, and the Vulgate produced bodily resurrection and Christological redemption (Redemptor meus vivit / in carne mea videbo Deum meum). This convergence of independent traditions all transforming the same passage reveals that the text's ambiguity was not an obstacle but an invitation — each tradition recognized that the MT's unresolved syntax was a lacuna to be filled with its own theological necessity. This has profound implications for understanding how canonical texts acquire their authority: it is not stability but productive instability that enables theological appropriation.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The famous verse 'I know that my Redeemer lives' in Job 19 was so ambiguous in Hebrew that Greek, Aramaic, and Latin translators all rewrote it differently — each to match their own community's most important belief about resurrection or Christ. This shows that the verse's power in religious tradition comes precisely from its original ambiguity.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis correctly identifies major well-known features of LXX Job (shorter text, wife's expanded speech, colophon, tiqqun in 1:5) but contains several questionable specific citations, a misquoted Greek text, and one inverted Ketiv/Qere claim that requires correction.

flagged_claims.claim: ἀναστήσει δέ μου τὸ δέρμα τὸ ἀναντλοῦν ταῦτα· παρὰ γὰρ Κυρίου ταῦτά μοι συνετελέσθη
flagged_claims.reason: This is not an accurate quotation of LXX Job 19:25-26. The actual LXX reads something like 'οἶδα γὰρ ὅτι ἀέναός ἐστιν ὁ ἐκλύειν με μέλλων ἐπὶ γῆς, ἀναστήσαι τὸ δέρμα μου τὸ ἀνατλῶν ταῦτα.' The quoted Greek appears partially fabricated or conflated.

flagged_claims.claim: Ketiv: לֹא יְיַחֵל ('he will not hope'), Qere: לוֹ אֲיַחֵל ('in him I will hope')
flagged_claims.reason: The Ketiv/Qere assignment is partially inverted/garbled. The standard Masoretic situation is Ketiv לֹא ('not') with Qere לוֹ ('to him/in him'), but the verb form analysis (יְיַחֵל third person vs. אֲיַחֵל first person) is conflated incorrectly across the two readings.

flagged_claims.claim: Schaper, Eschatology in the Greek Psalter, pp. 17–23
flagged_claims.reason: Schaper's monograph 'Eschatology in the Greek Psalter' (1995) is real, but it focuses on Psalms, not Job. Citing it for LXX Job 19:25 and 42:17 is at best tangential and the specific page range is suspicious as it is repeated across multiple unrelated claims.

flagged_claims.claim: Spittler, 'The Limits of Ecstasy', in Current Issues in Biblical and Patristic Interpretation
flagged_claims.reason: This citation appears fabricated or garbled. Russell Spittler's known work on Job concerns the Testament of Job (in OTP); 'The Limits of Ecstasy' is not a known title relevant to LXX Job 42:17.

flagged_claims.claim: van der Kooij, The Oracle of Tyre, pp. 12–18 (on LXX colophon technique)
flagged_claims.reason: Van der Kooij's 'The Oracle of Tyre' (1998) treats LXX Isaiah 23, not Job colophons. This citation is misapplied.

flagged_claims.claim: de Waard, A Handbook on the Book of Job, pp. 38–40
flagged_claims.reason: A UBS Handbook on Job exists (Rop & de Waard), but the 'principle of intentional expansion for theological clarification' attributed to de Waard is not a recognized named principle and may be invented.
Seow's Illuminations commentary on Job 1-21 exists, but page references should be verified; 837-845 is plausible for ch. 19 but should be checked against the actual edition.

flagged_claims.claim: cited by Origen as a genuine LXX reading
flagged_claims.reason: Origen's Hexapla marked LXX Job pluses with asterisks/obeli precisely because they were NOT in the Hebrew; characterizing this as Origen affirming it as 'genuine LXX' oversimplifies and risks misrepresenting Origen's text-critical practice.

flagged_claims.claim: patristic writers like Chrysostom to call her 'the devil's assistant'
flagged_claims.reason: Augustine famously called Job's wife 'diaboli adiutrix,' not Chrysostom. This appears to be a misattribution.

While ברך as euphemism for קלל in Job 1-2 is widely discussed, whether these specific Job instances belong to the classical lists of tiqqune sopherim is debated; the standard tiqqun sopherim lists do not typically include Job 1:5.

safe_claims: LXX Job is approximately one-sixth shorter than MT Job
LXX Job 2:9 contains a substantial expansion of Job's wife's speech
LXX Job 42:17 contains a colophon identifying Job with Jobab and referencing resurrection
MT Job 13:15 contains a Ketiv/Qere variation between לא and לו
The Hebrew of Job 1:5 uses ברך as a euphemism, traditionally understood to mean 'curse'
The MT of Job 19:25-27 is textually and syntactically difficult
